lessons.body: NGG helps young people aged 10–17 grow in character, competence and contribution. Saturdays are where development is practised; mentoring is where it is noticed and named.
You are one of three adults around each young person: their guardian, their centre team and you. You don't replace any of them.

quiz.q: Where is development mostly practised at NGG?
quiz.why: Saturdays are the development lab. Mentoring helps the young person notice and build on it.

lessons.body: Matches that start with friendship and trust last longer and do more good than matches that start with fixing problems. Spend the first month getting to know them.
Short, regular contact matters more than long, rare meetings. Matches that end early can leave a young person worse off than having no mentor, so only commit to what you can keep.

quiz.q: A new mentee is quiet in your first meeting. What helps most?
options: Do something together and let them lead the talk
quiz.why: Youth-led, activity-based time builds trust. Goals come after.

lessons.body: Be on time, every time. If you can't make it, tell the coordinator and the young person through the portal.
Ask open questions. Repeat back what you heard. Don't judge what they tell you.

quiz.q: You can't make Saturday. What do you do?
options: Tell the coordinator and message through the portal
quiz.why: All contact goes through the portal, and the coordinator can arrange cover.

lessons.body: Safeguarding is everyone's job. If you are worried about a young person, you must report it the same day. You do not need proof, and you must not investigate yourself.
Changes in mood, behaviour or appearance; unexplained injuries; fear of going home; talk of harm; sudden withdrawal from the group.

lessons.h: If a young person tells you something
lessons.body: Stay calm and listen. Don't promise to keep it secret. Say you'll need to tell someone whose job is to help. Write down their words, the date and time, then report through the portal.

scenario.situation: Mariam says: “If I tell you something, promise you won't tell anyone?”

options.why: You can't keep this promise if she's at risk. Breaking it later damages trust more.

options.text: “I can't promise that. If you're in danger, I'll need to tell someone whose job is to help. You can still talk to me.”
options.why: Honest and kind. She can decide what to say knowing the truth.
She's chosen this moment. Putting it off can mean she never tells anyone.

quiz.q: You're worried but have no proof. What do you do?
options: Report it today through the portal
quiz.why: Report concerns, not certainties. The safeguarding officer decides what happens next.

quiz.q: A young person discloses harm. What do you write down?
options: Their exact words, date and time
Nothing until you've asked more questions
quiz.why: Their words, unchanged. Don't lead or question further.

lessons.body: Only at the centre or in the NGG call room. Never alone off-site, never at your home or theirs, never in your car.
Don't give or lend money. Small, equal gifts only through the centre, such as a book at the end of term.
Handshakes and high-fives in public. No private jokes, nicknames or comments about appearance.

scenario.situation: Tolulope's parent asks if you can drive her home after the session because it's raining.

options.why: Mentors don't transport mentees. It protects both of you.

options.text: Say no kindly and ask the centre lead to help arrange safe transport
options.why: The centre has a process for this.

options.text: Give her money for a taxi
options.why: No money changes hands between mentor and mentee.

quiz.q: Where can you meet your mentee?
options: Only at the centre or the NGG call room
At their home with a parent present
quiz.why: Meeting places are fixed so everyone knows where young people are.

lessons.body: Message only through the NGG portal. No WhatsApp, Instagram, TikTok or phone calls. Messages are kept and can be seen by the safeguarding team.
Between 8am and 8pm. If a young person messages late, reply the next morning.
Don't take or share photos of a young person on your own phone. The centre handles photos with media consent.

scenario.situation: Kelechi sends you a friend request on Instagram.

options.why: Personal social media is off limits, even if it seems friendly.
Better to explain, so he doesn't feel rejected.

options.text: Decline and explain in the portal that you only chat on NGG

quiz.q: A mentee messages at 10pm. What do you do?
quiz.why: Keep to the hours. If it's urgent or worrying, report it.

lessons.body: Tap Report a concern, pick a category and write what happened. It goes straight to the safeguarding officer.
If a child is in immediate danger, call 112 first, then the safeguarding officer.

quiz.q: A child is in immediate danger. First step?
quiz.why: Emergency services first, then the officer.

lessons.body: Express care, challenge growth, provide support, share power, expand possibilities.
Help them work out what they think. “What would you do differently?” beats “You should…”

options: Letting them pick what you work on next
quiz.why: Young people grow more when they help decide.

lessons.body: Voice, courage, thinking, creativity, collaboration, responsibility, character, identity, initiative, reflection. Four levels: not seen, emerging, demonstrated, exemplary.

lessons.h: Rate what you saw, not who they are
lessons.body: Rate today's behaviour. A quiet day doesn't make a quiet child.
For any rise or for exemplary, write what they did: “Volunteered to present first.” Not “Excellent.”

scenario.situation: You want to rate Ibrahim's Initiative as Exemplary. Which evidence works?

options.why: Says how good, not what happened.

options.text: “Noticed his group had no plan, wrote one on the board and gave each person a job.”
options.why: Specific and observable. Another mentor would rate it the same.
About who he is, not what he did today.

quiz.why: Rises and exemplary ratings must be backed by what you saw.

lessons.body: The journal is private unless they choose to share. You only see what they share with you.
Reply briefly and warmly. Ask one question. Never correct spelling or grammar.

quiz.q: A mentee shares a journal entry. Best reply?

lessons.body: Name what they did, why it mattered and one thing to try next, on the same day.

options: “You explained your idea clearly; next time try looking at the group”

lessons.body: Keep showing up. Send one short message a week. Tell the coordinator after two weeks of silence.
Stay calm, separate if needed, and hear each side privately. Log it.

quiz.q: A mentee hasn't replied for two weeks. What now?
quiz.why: Coordinators help re-engage. Don't go round the portal.

lessons.body: Abrupt endings can hurt. A planned ending, with time to say goodbye, protects what you built.
Tell the coordinator first. Agree a last meeting. Review their goals and achievements together. Write a final note. Say goodbye properly, even if you're staying at NGG.
Don't just stop turning up. Don't promise to stay in touch outside NGG.

scenario.situation: You're moving to Abuja next month. When do you tell Tolulope?

options.text: On the last Saturday, so she isn't upset for weeks
options.why: A surprise ending feels like rejection.

options.text: After telling the coordinator, with at least three weeks to plan a proper goodbye
options.why: Time to review, celebrate and hand over.

options.text: Not at all, the coordinator will tell her
options.why: She should hear it from you, with support.

quiz.q: Who do you tell first about ending a match?
quiz.why: The coordinator plans the closure with you.

quiz.q: Which is part of a good closure?
options: Reviewing their goals and achievements together

lessons.body: New this year: voice notes are allowed in the portal. They are kept like messages. Video calls only in the NGG call room, which is recorded.

quiz.q: Where can you video call a mentee?
quiz.why: Only the NGG call room, which is recorded.
